posts.headline: Medicare negotiated drug list updated November 2026
posts.subhead: New deselections and 2028 price facts added
changes: New fact sheet and infographic published for negotiated prices taking effect in 2028
By March 1, 2027, CMS will post a price explanation for each drug with an agreed price for 2028
Five more drugs deselected: Farxiga, Januvia, Janumet/Janumet XR, Ofev, and Pomalyst removed January 1, 2028
Xeljanz/Xeljanz XR and Xolair deselected with removal effective January 1, 2029
posts.verdict_text: People on Medicare Part D or Part B who take these drugs should check whether negotiated prices still apply to their medication.
actions: Check if your drug is on the updated negotiated price list at Medicare.gov
Ask your pharmacist whether your drug's negotiated price still applies in 2027 or 2028
Call 1-800-MEDICARE or NJ SHIP at 1-800-792-8820 with coverage questions
posts.caption: CMS updated the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation page on November 23, 2026, adding new fact sheets and an infographic for negotiated prices that take effect in 2028. Several drugs have been deselected from the program: Farxiga, Januvia, Janumet, Janumet XR, Ofev, and Pomalyst will no longer carry negotiated prices starting January 1, 2028, and Xeljanz, Xeljanz XR, and Xolair follow on January 1, 2029. If you are on Medicare and take any of these drugs, check Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE to understand what this means for your costs. NJ residents can also reach NJ SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.
posts.video_script: Here is an update Medicare beneficiaries in New Jersey should know about. CMS just updated its negotiated drug price list in November 2026. Several drugs, including Farxiga, Januvia, Janumet, Ofev, and Pomalyst, have been removed from the negotiated price program starting January 1, 2028. Xeljanz and Xolair follow in 2029. If you or someone you care for takes any of these medications, now is the time to check your coverage. Full breakdown in the carousel - follow at N J care compass for the next change.

categories.explanation: Multiple drugs are being removed from the Medicare negotiated price program, meaning the lower Maximum Fair Price will no longer apply to those medications after their removal dates.

posts.headline: Caring for someone in New Jersey? Start here.
posts.subhead: You don't have to figure out every service on your own.
changes: New Jersey's new Caregiver Support Hub puts resources, training and support information in one place.

posts.headline: Home for Thanksgiving? Notice gently.
posts.subhead: A visit can make slow changes easier to spot.
changes: Around the house: little or expired food, unopened mail or unpaid bills, more clutter, missed or mixed-up medications.
Health and getting around: noticeable weight change, falls or trouble walking, clothes that don't suit the weather.
Memory and mood: memory slips that disrupt daily life, trouble with familiar tasks, confusion about the day, mood changes.
These can have other causes, like depression, infection or medications. A doctor's visit is the right first step.
One sign isn't a verdict. Jot down what you noticed and compare notes with siblings after the holiday, not at the table.
Start small: pick a quiet moment, ask instead of accuse, and offer one practical help, like grocery delivery or a ride.
posts.verdict_text: Talking early, while your parent can help decide, keeps more options open: help at home, adult day, respite care or assisted living.
actions: Save this for the drive home
posts.caption_rendered:
Thanksgiving is often the first time in months that families are all in one room. If something about Mom or Dad seems different this year, you're not imagining it, and you're not alone.

Swipe for what to notice and how to start the conversation, gently. One change doesn't mean a crisis. It means it's time to pay attention, compare notes with family, and plan the next talk.

November is National Family Caregivers Month. If you're already helping a parent, you're a caregiver too.

Free help in NJ: 877-222-3737 (your county's Aging & Disability Resource Connection) · Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline: 800-272-3900.
If someone says they feel hopeless or have no reason to live, call or text 988.

Sources: National Institute on Aging, "What Are the Signs That an Aging Parent Needs Help?"; Alzheimer's Association, 10 Warning Signs of Alzheimer's; NJ Department of Human Services. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

#NJCaregivers #NorthJersey #AgingParents #Caregiving #Thanksgiving #FamilyCaregiversMonth #ElderCare #NJCareCompass

posts.headline: Your parent's 2027 Medicare and Social Security numbers
posts.subhead: Both changes are final and start in January.
changes: Social Security benefits rise 3.6% in January 2027. The average retirement benefit goes up about $75 a month.
The standard Medicare Part B premium rises to $209.40 a month, up $6.50 from $202.90.
The Part B deductible rises to $292 (from $283). The Part A hospital deductible is $1,776 per benefit period.
COLA notices arrive in December by mail, unless your parent chose online notices in my Social Security.
posts.verdict_text: Part B usually comes out of the Social Security check, so the raise your parent actually sees will be a little smaller than 3.6%. Higher-income beneficiaries pay more for Part B.
actions: Check the new amount in my Social Security
Watch for the COLA notice in December
posts.caption_rendered:
New year, new numbers. Social Security benefits rise 3.6% in January, and the standard Medicare Part B premium rises to $209.40 a month. Because Part B usually comes out of the Social Security check, the increase your parent actually sees will be a little smaller.

Swipe for the 2027 figures and what to watch for in the mail.

Free Medicare help in NJ: SHIP, 1-800-792-8820.

Sources: Social Security Administration, COLA announcement, Oct 14, 2026; CMS, 2027 Medicare Part B and Part A notices, Nov 17, 2026. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: Recall: about 338,800 DREO space heaters
posts.subhead: They can overheat and catch fire.
changes: Model DR-HSH015: a black ceramic heater, about 11.5 inches wide by 13 inches tall, with a remote.
Only units made April 2025 through January 2026. Check the label underneath for date codes 2025/04 to 2026/01.
Sold at Costco and online at Dreo.com, Best Buy, Kohl's, Lowe's, QVC, Home Depot and others, $70 to $110.
DREO received 17 reports of the heaters igniting, including 3 with property damage and 1 burn injury.
posts.verdict_text: Stop using a recalled heater now. DREO offers a free replacement: you'll be asked to unplug it, cut the cord and send a photo.
posts.caption_rendered:
If your parent keeps a small heater by the chair or bed, check it this weekend. DREO is recalling about 338,800 DR-HSH015 space heaters because they can overheat and ignite.

Flip the heater over: if the model is DR-HSH015 and the date code is between 2025/04 and 2026/01, stop using it and contact DREO for a free replacement.

For any space heater this winter: plug it straight into the wall (not an extension cord), keep it 3 feet from beds, curtains and papers, turn it off when leaving the room or going to sleep, and make sure smoke alarms work.

Source: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, DREO space heater recall, Oct 29, 2026. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: One week left to change Medicare plans for 2027
changes: Plans change costs, covered drugs and networks every year. Changes made now take effect January 1, 2027.
Start with the Annual Notice of Change your parent's plan mailed this fall. It lists what's different.
Are all their prescriptions still covered, and at what cost? Are their doctors and pharmacy still in network?
Pushy sales calls ramp up now. Medicare won't call out of the blue to sell a plan. Hang up and call 1-800-MEDICARE.
posts.verdict_text: Anyone with Medicare can switch plans until December 7. People already in Medicare Advantage get another chance to switch January 1 to March 31.
posts.caption_rendered:
Medicare open enrollment closes Monday, Dec 7. If your parent takes several medications or sees specialists, a 20-minute check now can save surprises in January.

Swipe for what to look at, and how to spot the sales calls that flood in this time of year.

Free help: NJ SHIP, 1-800-792-8820 (they don't sell anything).

Sources: CMS, 2027 Medicare Open Enrollment dates (Oct 15 – Dec 7, 2026); SSA, Medicare Open Enrollment reminder, Nov 16, 2026. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: Recall: Xentrawave adult bed rails
posts.subhead: A person can get trapped in or beside the rail. One death has been reported.
changes: Model XT016, all batches, and model XT026, batch 20251212 only. Model number is on the box and manual.
Black or gray metal frame, gray foam grips, gray fabric pouch with a green "Xentrawave" label.
Sold on Amazon.com, May 2025 through August 2026, for about $37 to $40. About 2,114 sold.
For any portable bed rail: check for gaps between the rail and mattress, and keep the retention strap attached.
posts.verdict_text: Stop using a recalled rail now and contact Xentrawave for a full refund. You'll be asked to cut the foam grips and send a photo.
actions: Look up any bed rail brand at cpsc.gov/recalls
Ask a doctor or OT if a rail is right for your parent
posts.caption_rendered:
Bed rails are meant to help, but the wrong one, or one with a gap, can trap a person. CPSC has recalled Xentrawave XT016 bed rails (all batches) and XT026 rails from batch 20251212, sold on Amazon. One death has been reported.

Swipe for how to identify the rail, what to do, and a quick check for any bed rail in your parent's home.

Source: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, Xentrawave adult portable bed rail recall (27-099), Nov 19, 2026. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: Scams against older adults: the new FTC numbers
posts.subhead: What the report found, and a simple plan to make with your parent.
changes: Adults 60+ reported about $3 billion in fraud losses in 2025. The FTC estimates the true cost may be far higher.
People 80 and older who lost money reported a median loss of $2,000.
Older adults were more likely to report losing money to tech-support, prize and government-impersonation scams.
Warning signs: urgency, secrecy, and payment by gift card, wire, crypto or cash handed to a courier.
posts.verdict_text: Hang up and call back on a number you already trust: the one on the card, statement or official website. Never use a number from the message itself.
actions: Agree on a family code word
Ask your parent to call you before sending money
posts.caption_rendered:
The FTC's new report to Congress says adults 60 and older reported about $3 billion in fraud losses in 2025, and people 80 and older who lost money reported a median loss of $2,000. The holidays bring more calls, texts and pop-ups.

Swipe for the scams to know, the warning signs, and a simple plan to make with your parent. Keep it calm: anyone can be targeted.

Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov or to the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs. If money was sent, call the bank or card company right away.

Source: Federal Trade Commission, Protecting Older Consumers 2025–2026, report to Congress, October 2026; FTC consumer alert, November 2026. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: Caregivers need breaks too
posts.subhead: That's what respite care is for.
changes: Respite care is short-term care for your parent so you can rest, run errands, work or travel.
It can be a few hours or a few days: an aide at home, an adult day program, or a short stay in a care facility.
NJ's Statewide Respite Care Program helps eligible families with respite costs.
It has financial eligibility rules. Your county office can tell you whether your family qualifies.
posts.verdict_text: Taking a break isn't giving up. Rested caregivers give better care, and stay caregivers longer.
actions: Ask about the Statewide Respite Care Program
Save this for when you need it
posts.caption_rendered:
If you've been the one handling every appointment, call and meal, you're allowed to step away. Respite care covers your parent for a few hours or a few days so you can recharge.

New Jersey's Statewide Respite Care Program can help eligible families. Start with your county office: 877-222-3737.

Source: NJ Department of Human Services, Division of Aging Services, Statewide Respite Care Program. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: Holidays bring family together. Use 30 minutes well.
posts.subhead: A simple agenda for a family check-in about Mom or Dad.
changes: Health: upcoming appointments and who can go, the current medication list, and anything that's changed.
Money and mail: are bills getting paid? Who can help? Any odd calls, charges or "prizes"?
Home: stairs, rugs, lighting, grab bars. Is driving still safe? Who checks in between visits?
Papers: is there a health care proxy and power of attorney, and where are they? Who has insurance card copies?
posts.verdict_text: Living far away doesn't mean you can't help. Split tasks by what each person can actually do from where they live, and include your parent: it's their life.
actions: Set a date for the next family call
posts.caption_rendered:
Living far away doesn't mean you can't help. The holidays may be the only time everyone is in the same place, so use 30 minutes of it well.

Swipe for a simple check-in agenda: health, money, home, papers, and who does what. Include your parent in the conversation. It's their life.

Free NJ help: 877-222-3737.

Sources: National Institute on Aging, "Getting Started with Long-Distance Caregiving"; NJ Department of Human Services. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: Traveling with Mom or Dad this season?
posts.subhead: A little planning makes the trip easier for everyone.
changes: Book nonstop flights when you can, travel at your parent's best time of day, and leave room for rest.
Carry-on, not checked: medications in labeled bottles plus extra days, a medication list, and insurance cards.
Call the airline ahead to request a wheelchair or boarding help. TSA Cares (855-787-2227) wants 72 hours' notice.
On long trips, get up and move often and drink water. Ask the doctor about compression stockings.
If memory is a concern, keep routines familiar and make sure your parent carries ID and an emergency contact.
When you arrive: check for loose rugs and cords, and add a night-light on the path to the bathroom.
posts.verdict_text: Original Medicare covers care anywhere in the U.S. Medicare Advantage plans may limit out-of-network care, so call the plan before an out-of-state trip.
posts.caption_rendered:
Holiday travel is hard enough. Add a parent who tires easily, takes several medications or gets confused in new places, and it takes real planning.

Swipe for what to pack, how to get help at the airport, what to watch for on long drives, and the insurance question to ask before you leave.

Two numbers worth saving:
TSA Cares, 855-787-2227. Call at least 72 hours before a flight to request help at security.
NJ SHIP, 1-800-792-8820. Free Medicare counseling, including what's covered when you travel.

Caring for someone with memory loss? The Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline is 800-272-3900.

Sources: TSA (Passenger Support / TSA Cares); U.S. DOT, Air Carrier Access Act guidance; Medicare.gov; Alzheimer's Association, Traveling and Dementia. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: Hiring home care for a parent? Ask these first.
posts.subhead: A good agency will be glad you asked.
changes: Are you registered with NJ Consumer Affairs? Every agency that places aides in NJ homes must be.
Are your aides certified home health aides (CHHA) in New Jersey, and do you verify it with the Board of Nursing?
Are aides your employees or contractors? It affects who pays taxes and carries insurance.
Who supervises care? NJ agencies must have a licensed health care supervisor, such as a registered nurse.
What happens if the aide can't come? Ask about backup coverage, minimum hours and changing aides.
posts.verdict_text: Bringing someone into your parent's home is a big decision. Checking registration first protects your parent and gives you somewhere to turn if something goes wrong.
actions: Get costs and cancellation terms in writing
posts.caption_rendered:
Bringing someone into your parent's home is a big decision. A good agency will be glad you asked these questions.

Swipe for five to ask before you sign, starting with one many families skip: is the agency registered with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs? Every health care service firm that places aides in NJ homes must be.

Check registration: NJ Division of Consumer Affairs, Regulated Business Section, 973-504-6370.

Source: NJ Division of Consumer Affairs, Health Care Service Firms. Last checked Nov 23, 2026. Independent, not a government office.

posts.headline: Holidays when a parent has dementia
posts.subhead: Small changes can make the season easier for everyone.
changes: Keep the routine: usual mealtimes and bedtimes, and visits at your parent's best time of day.
Smaller is better: fewer guests, less noise, shorter visits, and a quiet room they can go to.
Prepare guests ahead of time. Suggest they introduce themselves and keep conversation simple.
Include them with a familiar, simple job: folding napkins, stirring, or looking at old photos together.

actions: Share this with family before the visit

changes: About $38 an hour: the 2025 statewide median for home health aide care in New Jersey (CareScout).

Medicare usually won't pay for ongoing help with daily activities like bathing and dressing.
Medicaid, VA benefits or long-term care insurance may help, depending on eligibility.

posts.headline: Look up any nursing home before you visit
posts.subhead: Four checks that take under ten minutes.
changes: Check the 1-to-5 star rating: it combines health inspections, staffing, and quality measures in one score.
Read the last three years of health inspection reports to see citations, what was wrong, and whether it was fixed.
Check staffing: look for nurse hours per resident per day and staff turnover — more hours, less turnover is better.
Look for any Medicare penalties — a fine or denied payment — listed on the facility's Care Compare page.
posts.verdict_text: A quick Care Compare search before you visit can reveal inspection citations, low staffing, or Medicare penalties that a tour alone will not show.
actions: Search any NJ nursing home free at medicare.gov/care-compare
Call NJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995 (all NJ counties)
File a care complaint with NJ Dept. of Health: 1-800-792-9770
posts.caption_rendered:
BEFORE YOU CHOOSE

Before you tour a nursing home in Bergen, Essex, Hudson, Morris, Passaic, Sussex, Union, or Warren County, spend a few minutes on Care Compare. The free federal tool shows you each facility's star rating across three areas: health inspections, staffing levels, and quality measures. You can read the actual inspection reports from the past three years, see how many nurse hours per day each resident receives on average, check staff turnover rates, and find out whether Medicare has ever fined or penalized the facility. None of that shows up on a lobby tour. Use what you find online to form sharper questions when you walk in the door. Source: Medicare.gov Care Compare.
